questions.q: Which of these is a proposition?
questions.explain: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. "The balance is at least ₦5,000" is one. A question with a number as its answer, an instruction, or a bare value is not.
options: How much money is in the account?

questions.q: What kind of value does balance >= amount produce?
questions.explain: Every comparison operator (>, >=, <, <=, ===, !==) answers a yes/no question, so it produces a boolean.
options: A number: the difference between the two
The larger of the two numbers

questions.q: Which variable name best fits a boolean that says whether a customer may withdraw?
questions.explain: Boolean names should read as a yes/no question: canWithdraw, isActive, hasEnoughMoney. withdraw sounds like an action, and a double negative like isNotUnableToWithdraw forces the reader to flip it twice.

questions.q: In the truth table of a && b, how many of the four rows are true?
questions.explain: AND is true only when both inputs are true, which is one row out of four. That strictness is why AND suits permission to do something risky.

questions.q: In the truth table of a || b, how many of the four rows are true?
questions.explain: OR is false only when both inputs are false. The other three rows, including "both true", are true.

questions.q: When is a XOR b true?
questions.explain: Exclusive or means one or the other, but not both and not neither. Equivalently: the two inputs are different.
options: When at least one is true

questions.q: payByCard and payByTransfer are booleans. Which expression is true when exactly one payment method is chosen?
questions.explain: XOR is true when the two inputs differ, and !== on two booleans says exactly that. || would also accept both methods at once, which would charge the customer twice.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say not to use ^ for boolean XOR?
questions.explain: ^ is bitwise XOR: true ^ false is 1. Use a !== b on real booleans. Powers are written **.
options: It does not exist in JavaScript
It works on the bits of numbers and returns a number, such as 1, not a boolean

questions.q: A shipping rule depends on five true/false inputs. How many rows does its full truth table have?
questions.explain: Each input doubles the number of rows: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 25 = 32.

questions.q: Why does adding one more boolean input double the number of truth-table rows?
questions.explain: Every old combination is still possible, and each can now be paired with either value of the new input. Two copies of every row: the count doubles.
options: Because each input adds two new rows at the end
Because every existing row now appears once with the new input false and once with it true
Because truth tables always have an even number of rows
Because AND and OR each need their own copy

questions.q: How does JavaScript group a || b && c?
questions.explain: && binds before ||, like multiplication before addition. Add parentheses whenever you mix them, so no reader has to remember this.
options: Left to right, so (a || b) && c
It is a syntax error without parentheses

questions.q: The business says: "Admins can always edit an order. Owners can edit it only before it ships." Which expression says that?
questions.explain: Admin alone is enough, so it sits on one side of an OR. The owner case needs two things, so it is an AND group. The first option would stop admins editing shipped orders: a different rule.

questions.q: A code review finds if (isAdmin || true) { deleteUser(); }. What does the condition simplify to?
questions.explain: a || true is always true: one way in that always works opens the door to everyone. The author almost certainly left a debugging shortcut in.

questions.q: What can you say about the code inside if (isOpen && !isOpen) { … }?
questions.explain: a && !a is always false: nothing is true and false at once. The block is dead code, which usually means the author typed the wrong variable.
options: It runs only when the shop is open
It runs only when the shop is closed

questions.q: Which expression is always equal to a, whatever boolean a is?
questions.explain: Adding a condition that always holds changes nothing, so a && true is a. The others are always false, always true and always true.

questions.q: "If the film is age-restricted, the customer must be 18 or older." Which expression is true exactly when this requirement is met?
questions.explain: The requirement fails only when the film is restricted and the customer is not an adult. In every other case it holds, which is "not restricted, or adult". restricted && isAdult would wrongly refuse children at unrestricted films.

questions.q: The cash machine bug (|| instead of &&) passed testing. What testing habit would have caught it?
questions.explain: The tested accounts were "fully fine" and "fully closed", where AND and OR agree. The bug lived in the two rows nobody tried. A rule with two inputs has only four rows, so test them all.
options: Testing with larger amounts of money
Testing every row of the rule's truth table, not only a few chosen accounts
Testing only accounts that are fully fine

questions.q: Which of these values is truthy?
questions.explain: The falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined and NaN. "false" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy, a classic trap when a form or a file sends booleans as text.

questions.q: Before combining inputs with logic, the lesson turns itemsInCart into itemsInCart > 0. Why?
questions.explain: && and || return one of their values, and !== on a string and a number just asks whether they differ. Comparisons give real booleans, and boolean logic is only reliable on booleans.
options: Because logic on raw values can return non-booleans and give wrong answers, for example with !== as XOR

questions.q: A user record has no isBlocked field, so user.isBlocked is undefined. Which login check falls to the safe side?
questions.explain: Only an explicit false should let the user in. !undefined is true and undefined !== true is true, so the first and third checks treat "we don't know" as "not blocked". The last one lets everyone in.

questions.q: A condition has grown to ten boolean inputs. What does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: Ten inputs mean 210 = 1,024 cases. Naming sub-rules such as const canManageFile = isOwner || isAdmin; keeps each piece small enough to reason about and test.
options: Test a few rows at random
Split it into named pieces, each small enough to check fully
Replace && with || to make it shorter
Remove the parentheses so it fits on one line

questions.explain: a must be true (4 rows left). Among those, b || c is false only when both are false, so 3 of the 4 remain.

questions.q: && and || return one of their values. What does this print?
questions.explain: && stops at the first falsy value and returns it: 0. In the second line the string is truthy, so it returns the right side, the boolean 0 > 0, which is false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: On raw values, a string is always different from a number, so the first line is true. On real booleans, both are present (true !== true), so "exactly one" is correctly false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The field is missing, so it is undefined. !undefined is true, but undefined === false is false: "unknown" is not the same as "no".

questions.q: Chaining XOR is not "exactly one". What does this print?
questions.explain: It is read left to right: true !== true is false, then false !== true is true. A chain of XORs is true when an odd number of inputs are true, so all three methods pass. Count instead.

questions.q: This loop checks one expression for both values of a. What does it print?
questions.explain: a || !a is always true and a && !a is always false. A two-row loop is a complete proof, because a has no other values.
options:
false true false
true true false

false false false
true true true

false true true
true true false

false false true
true true false

questions.q: Finish canWithdraw(isActive, isLocked, balance, amount): withdrawal is allowed when the account is active, not locked, and the balance is at least the amount.
questions.explain: Three conditions that must all hold: a chain of &&. "Not locked" is !isLocked, and "at least" is >=.

questions.q: Use two nested for … of [false, true] loops to print the truth table of OR, one row per line, as a b result (for example false true true).
questions.explain: The outer loop holds a while the inner one tries both values of b, giving the four rows in the usual order.

questions.q: Write validPayment(card, transfer) that returns true only when exactly one payment method is chosen.
questions.explain: "Exactly one of two" is XOR, and XOR on two booleans is "they are different": card !== transfer.

questions.q: Free delivery is given when (bigOrder || isPremium) && inLagos. Loop over all 8 combinations of the three inputs and print how many rows give free delivery, as free in N of 8 rows.
questions.explain: inLagos must be true (4 rows), and of those, bigOrder || isPremium fails only when both are false. So 3 rows.

questions.q: Write exactlyOne(card, transfer, wallet) that returns true only when exactly one of the three booleans is true. Count the true values; do not chain !==.
questions.explain: "Exactly one of many" is a counting question. A chained !== would say true for all three, because three is odd.

questions.q: Test two versions of the withdrawal rule against the expected table. For each of the four rows, print ok when buggy gives the expected answer and FAIL otherwise.
questions.explain: Each row holds the inputs and the answer the business rule demands. Destructuring takes a row apart, and a comparison with === checks it. The buggy OR fails the two mixed rows.

questions.q: The business rule is: "nobody may edit a shipped order; otherwise admins and owners may edit". The code below gets it wrong for a shipped order with an admin. Fix canEdit with parentheses so it prints false, then true.
questions.explain: Without parentheses, && binds first, so the admin side escapes the shipping check. Grouping the OR makes "not shipped" apply to everyone.

questions.q: Prove the law "a && true equals a" by looping over both values of a and printing a and whether the law holds, one line per value.
questions.explain: A boolean has only two values, so checking both is a complete proof, not just a test.
